title: Episode 137: Abraham Lincoln and the Cooper Union Speech: Right Makes Might

In February eighteen sixty, Abraham Lincoln was an obscure Western politician. A one-term former congressman from the prairie frontier of Illinois, Lincoln was known nationally only for his losing eighteen fifty-eight Senate debates against Stephen A. Douglas. The undisputed front-runner for the Republican presidential nomination was New York's sophisticated, wealthy Senator William H. Seward, backed by the political machine of Thurlow Weed.

When a young men's Republican club invited Lincoln to deliver a lecture in New York City, Lincoln recognized it as the gamble of a lifetime. Arriving at the Astor House hotel, Lincoln was an awkward sight: six feet four inches tall, gaunt, wearing a brand-new black suit that arrived wrinkled from his trunk, with sleeves and trousers that were too short for his lanky frame. On the freezing night of February twenty-seventh, eighteen sixty, fifteen hundred of New York's cultural, literary, and financial elite packed the Great Hall of the Cooper Union to inspect the frontier curiosity.

What followed was one of the greatest forensic masterworks in American political history. Lincoln systematically analyzed the voting records of the thirty-nine signers of the Constitution, dismantling Southern claims that the founders considered slavery sacred. Concluding with the immortal rallying cry, 'Let us have faith that right makes might,' Lincoln electrified the hall and the national press. Three months later at the Chicago 'Wigwam' convention, Lincoln's team outmaneuvered Seward, securing the presidential nomination that would save the Union. Here is George with the story of the speech that made Lincoln President.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we begin our exploration of America's sixteenth President, Abraham Lincoln. Before he was the Great Emancipator, before he carried the nation through the crucible of civil war, Lincoln was an unpolished frontier lawyer with a high-pitched voice and a wrinkled suit. In February eighteen sixty, he walked into the heart of New York City's intellectual elite and delivered a speech of such transcendent moral and legal power that it changed the course of American history. Here is George with the story of the Cooper Union address.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: AN OBSCURE WESTERN FRONTIER LAWYER
In early eighteen sixty, the front-runner for the Republican nomination for President of the United States seemed unshakable. Senator William H. Seward of New York—former governor, brilliant orator, and champion of the 'Higher Law' against slavery—commanded the wealthy, powerful New York political machine directed by Thurlow Weed. To Eastern elites, the next President of the United States was already chosen.
A thousand miles to the west, in Springfield, Illinois, fifty-one-year-old Abraham Lincoln was quietly daring to dream an impossible dream. On paper, Lincoln's political credentials were microscopic: four terms in the Illinois state legislature and a single, undistinguished two-year term in the House of Representatives twelve years earlier. He had run for the United States Senate twice and lost both times. His fame rested entirely on his losing eighteen fifty-eight campaign against the titan Stephen A. Douglas, whose debates had been published in newspapers across the country.
In October eighteen fifty-nine, Lincoln received an unexpected letter from a young men's Republican committee in New York, inviting him to deliver a lecture as part of a winter lecture series at Henry Ward Beecher's Plymouth Church in Brooklyn, offering a speaking fee of two hundred dollars. Lincoln accepted instantly. He knew that if he was ever to be considered a serious dark-horse contender for the national ticket, he had to prove himself before the sophisticated, critical literary and political establishment of New York.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MONTHS IN THE LAW LIBRARY
Abraham Lincoln did not prepare for New York by writing applause lines or fiery stump slogans. He approached the assignment like a supreme constitutional advocate preparing a brief for the highest court in the land.
For three grueling months, during the freezing Illinois winter of eighteen fifty-nine and sixty, Lincoln virtually lived inside the Illinois State Capitol law library in Springfield. He called for trunk after trunk of colonial records, congressional journals, the Northwest Ordinance of seventeen eighty-seven, and the secret debates of the Constitutional Convention. He meticulously tabulated the individual voting records of every single one of the thirty-nine men who had signed the United States Constitution.
Lincoln's objective was to answer a central, deceitful claim made by Southern Democrats and Stephen Douglas. Douglas had repeatedly claimed that the founding fathers had established the principle of popular sovereignty, believing that the federal government had no constitutional right to restrict or prohibit slavery in federal territories. Lincoln was determined to test that claim against hard, historical evidence. He worked by candlelight late into the night, compiling names, dates, roll-call tallies, and presidential signatures, constructing an airtight, mathematical fortress of fact.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ARRIVAL AT THE ASTOR HOUSE
On February twenty-fifth, eighteen sixty, after a grueling three-day train journey across snowbound tracks, Abraham Lincoln arrived in New York City, checking into the elegant Astor House hotel on Broadway. Lincoln was an alarming, awkward sight in the fashionable metropolis. He stood six feet four inches tall—a towering giant in an era when the average man stood five feet seven—with long, dangling arms, enormous hands, hollow cheeks, and deep, melancholy gray eyes.
To prepare for his Eastern debut, Lincoln had purchased a brand-new suit of black broadcloth in Springfield. But the suit had been packed into his leather traveling valise, and when he unpacked it at the Astor House, the coat and trousers were a mass of heavy creases and wrinkles. Even worse, the tailor had cut the sleeves too short, exposing Lincoln's large bony wrists, and the trousers rode high above his boots.
Furthermore, Lincoln learned upon arrival that his venue had been moved. Because of intense public interest, the lecture had been relocated from Beecher's Brooklyn church to the Great Hall of the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art in Manhattan—a massive underground auditorium seating fifteen hundred people. Lincoln was terrified. He was an unpolished frontier lawyer about to speak before the most sophisticated, cynical, and educated audience in America.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GATHERING IN THE GREAT HALL
On the freezing, snow-covered evening of Monday, February twenty-seventh, eighteen sixty, fifteen hundred people packed the subterranean Great Hall of the Cooper Union. Admission was twenty-five cents. In the audience sat New York's cultural, financial, and intellectual royalty: prominent judges, Wall Street bankers, editors, and scholars, including the venerable poet William Cullen Bryant, editor of the New York Evening Post, and Horace Greeley, the influential editor of the New York Tribune.
When William Cullen Bryant introduced Lincoln, a ripple of uneasy skepticism passed through the crowd. Lincoln stepped to the podium looking awkward and uncomfortable. His wrinkled black suit hung loosely on his frame, his hair was unruly, and one of his stiff white shirt collars rode high on his neck. An eyewitness in the audience wrote that Lincoln looked like a backwoods rube who had wandered into an opera house.
When Lincoln began to speak, the initial impression grew worse. His voice was high-pitched, thin, and carried a sharp, distinctive frontier Kentucky twang that grated on refined Eastern ears. He seemed nervous, his hands shaking slightly as he adjusted his manuscript on the wooden lectern. Many in the audience looked at one another in disappointment, wondering how this ungainly Westerner had ever dared challenge Stephen Douglas. But then, as Lincoln warmed to his argument, a miraculous transformation occurred.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE HISTORICAL DISSECTION
Within five minutes, Lincoln's awkwardness vanished. His stooped posture straightened until he towered above the crowd, his gray eyes lit up with incandescent moral fire, and his voice deepened into a resonant, booming baritone that reached the farthest corner of the cavernous hall. The Great Hall fell into spellbound silence.
Lincoln took as his text a quote from Stephen Douglas: 'Our fathers, when they framed the government under which we live, understood this question just as well, and even better, than we do now.' Lincoln agreed with the premise—and then proceeded to systematically dismantle Douglas with his three months of library research.
With mathematical precision, Lincoln examined the thirty-nine signers of the Constitution. He proved that of the thirty-nine framers, twenty-one of them—an absolute majority—had voted on federal measures that restricted or prohibited slavery in federal territories, including George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and James Madison. In total, thirty-one of the thirty-nine had supported federal control over territorial slavery.
With devastating, surgical logic, Lincoln turned Douglas's argument against him. The founding fathers, Lincoln proved, had never intended slavery to be an eternal, sacred national institution. They had treated it as an evil to be tolerated where it existed, but strictly contained and marked for ultimate extinction. The audience, accustomed to flowery rhetorical bombs, was mesmerized by Lincoln's calm, relentless mastery of constitutional history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: RIGHT MAKES MIGHT
In the second half of his address, Lincoln turned his attention to the South. Speaking with profound, dispassionate calm, he addressed Southern threats of disunion. Southern radicals had warned that if a Republican was elected President, the South would secede and blame the North for the destruction of the Union.
Lincoln exposed the moral absurdity of this threat with a brilliant frontier parable: 'A highwayman holds a pistol to my ear, and mutters through his teeth, "Stand and deliver, or I shall kill you, and then you will be a murderer!" The threat was not my threat, but his; and the crime was not my crime, but his.' Lincoln declared that the South would never be satisfied with Northern silence; they demanded that the North declare slavery to be morally right.
Then came the magnificent, thunderous climax. Gathering his full height, his voice ringing with prophetic moral power, Lincoln delivered the words that would echo down the corridors of American memory:
'Neither let us be slandered from our duty by false accusations against us, nor frightened from it by menaces of destruction to the government, nor of dungeons to ourselves. Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.'
For a heartbeat, the hall was frozen in stunned silence. Then, fifteen hundred people leaped to their feet. Men threw their hats into the air, women waved white handkerchiefs, and the Great Hall erupted in a deafening, standing ovation that lasted for ten minutes. Horace Greeley leaned toward a colleague and declared: 'No man has made such an impression in New York since the days of Daniel Webster!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SPEECH THAT MADE LINCOLN PRESIDENT
The Cooper Union address was a political earthquake. The following morning, four major New York daily newspapers printed the full text of Lincoln's speech on their front pages. Over the next month, over one hundred thousand pamphlet copies were printed and distributed across the Northern states, read aloud at town halls and firesides from Maine to Minnesota.
Almost overnight, Lincoln was transformed from an obscure Illinois prairie lawyer into a first-rank national statesman. He demonstrated that he possessed what front-runner William H. Seward lacked: a dispassionate, unassailable conservative appeal rooted in the Constitution, paired with an unyielding moral core.
Three months later, in May eighteen sixty, ten thousand delegates and spectators packed the vast wooden convention hall known as the 'Wigwam' in Chicago for the Republican National Convention. Through masterly maneuvering by his campaign team, Lincoln's forces held Seward below a majority on the first two ballots. On the third ballot, the dam broke: state after state swung to Lincoln, and Abraham Lincoln was nominated for President of the United States.
Lincoln later acknowledged that the Cooper Union speech was the turning point of his life. He told friends: 'That speech made me President.'
In a single night in Manhattan, an unpolished frontier lawyer with wrinkled clothes and a high-pitched voice had proved that in a great republic, true power belongs not to wealth, pedigree, or political machines, but to the unshakeable force of moral truth. Right had made might—and the man who would save the Union was on his way to history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Abraham Lincoln's Cooper Union address launched his improbable journey to the White House and defined the moral spine of the American republic. Next week, we continue with Abraham Lincoln's second colossal chapter: the crucible of the Civil War, the drafting of the Emancipation Proclamation, and the immortal consecration of the battlefield at Gettysburg. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
